To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the anterior insula is activated by the suffering of others and predicts costly helping, whereas the nucleus accumbens is activated by the negative evaluation of others and predicts not helping, and 2) empathy and social evaluation are dissociated neural mechanisms that can predict prosocial behavior.
the willingness to engage is costly helping toward ingroups and outgroups is predicted by distinct neural responses to the suffering of ingroup members and outgroup members, respectively.
the willingness to help is predicted by the degree to which one feels empathy for the suffering of the person who needs help.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question whether the brain processes that precede costly helping are similar to those that precede costly harming.
the neurobiology of prosocial decisions and the role of perceived ingroup membership in these decisions.
social decision making and the neural mechanisms that support prosocial decisions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the anterior insula activation is associated with the willingness to help an ingroup member whereas the nucleus accumbens is associated with the unwillingness to help an outgroup member.
the anterior insula is involved in empathic concern for others' pain and that the nucleus accumbens is involved in the negative evaluation of others.
the anterior insula is involved in the perception of suffering, whereas the nucleus accumbens is involved in the decision to help.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
empathy is a crucial factor to understand the neural mechanisms underlying costly helping.
empathy-related insular activity is a key component in the decision to engage in costly prosocial behavior.
empathy and antagonism towards others are both important in determining prosocial behaviour.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the neural responses to ingroup and out-group members' suffering predict individual differences in helping behavior.
the brain's reward system can act as a brake on costly helping, whereas the brain's empathy system can act as an accelerator.
prosocial decisions are modulated by the social group to which the recipient of help belongs.
